topic: fitting a root cellar under an existing garden shed

provenance.author: glowny-en-b
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is spoil, block and crate arithmetic with closed task questions, base is an exploratory dialogue about digging, lining and venting the cellar. Grounded external referent: the vent, introduced in turn 0 (the plan hangs on one vent) and mentioned in the sentence directly before every insertion (low and high vent, ordered pipes, knee height, low vent fitted).

a: Here is the cellar dig under the shed, and the spoil volume needs working out first.
The pit is two metres long, one and a half metres wide, and two metres deep.
Spoil swells by a quarter once it is dug, so the barrow count must use the swollen figure.
The barrow takes eighty litres per load, filled level and no more.
How many cubic metres of spoil come out of the pit before any swelling?
base: We are putting a root cellar under the garden shed, and the digging starts this weekend.
The shed floor is up, the joists are propped, and the soil below is heavy clay.
The plan hangs on one vent, a pipe meant to pull cool night air down inside.
Everything we read says a cellar without moving air is just a cupboard of rot.
How deep does the pit really need to be for potatoes and apples to keep?

a: The pit holds six cubic metres of soil before any swelling is counted in.
Swollen by a quarter, the spoil becomes seven and a half cubic metres to move.
At eighty litres per level load, that is ninety-four barrow trips, rounding the last one up.
At three minutes per trip, the wheeling alone takes four hours and forty-two minutes.
Does the plan give one digger and one wheeler enough daylight for those trips?
base: Two metres is plenty, and in heavy clay the walls will stand while you line them.
The clay is your friend for temperature and your enemy for water, in equal measure.
One vent will not do, because air only moves when it has somewhere to leave.
You want a low vent bringing cool air in and a high one letting warm air out.
Where does the water table sit in that corner of the garden after a wet month?

a: Now count the blocks, because the walls are lined with concrete blocks laid flat.
The two long walls take forty blocks each, and the two short walls take thirty each.
Blocks arrive on pallets of sixty, and broken ones run at five per pallet on average.
Count usable blocks per pallet first, then the pallets the whole lining needs.
How many blocks in all do the four walls call for before breakage?
base: The water table stays well down even in winter, or the old soakaway would not work.
The vent pipes are ordered in the same width as the rainwater kind, ten centimetres.
We can run the low pipe from the north side and the high one through the roof.
The clay smells sour where we cut it, which the forum people say is normal.
Should the pit floor be left as bare clay or given a proper layer of something?

a: The four walls call for one hundred forty blocks before any breakage is counted.
A pallet of sixty gives fifty-five usable blocks once the average five broken are removed.
Two pallets give one hundred ten usable, which falls thirty short of the need.
Three pallets give one hundred sixty-five usable and cover the job with twenty-five spare.
Set the spare figure aside, because the shelf piers draw on it next.
Do the twenty-five spare blocks cover the two shelf piers at twelve blocks each?
base: Leave the middle of the floor as bare clay, but bed the walking line with loose gravel.
Bare clay breathes moisture your crops want, and gravel keeps your boots out of it.
Run the low vent right down to knee height, or the cool air will pool near the ceiling.
A mesh cap on both pipes keeps the mice out from the very first night.
Is the shed roof high enough to give the outlet pipe a decent rise outside?

a: One correction from the yard: breakage runs at eight blocks per pallet, not five.
Rework the usable count per pallet and check the three pallet plan again.
Give the new usable figure first and then the running totals pallet by pallet.
Keep the wall need at one hundred forty blocks exactly as before.
The shelf piers still want twelve blocks each from whatever remains spare.
Do three pallets still cover the walls and both piers after that change?
base: The shed roof gives the outlet a metre of rise, and we can add a cowl on top.
Today we cut the hatch opening in the floor and framed it with the old joist offcuts.
The hatch itself is just loose boards for now, resting on the frame.
The low vent is in, and the draught from it already smells of cold clay.
What should a proper hatch be lined with so it does not sweat and drip?

a: With eight broken, each pallet yields fifty-two usable blocks instead of fifty-five.
The running totals go fifty-two, then one hundred four, then one hundred fifty-six.
The walls take one hundred forty, leaving sixteen spare from three pallets.
The two piers want twenty-four together, so sixteen spare falls eight blocks short.
Loose blocks cost more each, but a pallet adds a delivery charge on top.
Should a fourth pallet be ordered, or just eight loose blocks from the yard?
base: Line the hatch with the same boards as the floor and glue cork sheet underneath.
Cork keeps the warm shed air from meeting a cold surface, which is where drip starts.
The high vent can share the cowl the chimney people sell for ten a piece.
Fit a simple bolt so the hatch cannot be lifted by a curious child.
What goes on the shelves first once the walls are dry enough to load?

a: Now plan the shelves, because each bay holds crates in three sizes.
A big crate is sixty centimetres wide, a middle one forty, and a small one thirty.
Each shelf run is one hundred eighty centimetres long between the piers.
Fill one run with big crates only and another with middle crates only.
How many middle crates fit along one run without any overhang at the ends?
base: Apples go in first on the top shelf, wrapped singly and away from everything else.
Apples breathe out something that wakes potatoes up, so distance and airflow matter.
Potatoes take the low shelves in paper sacks, folded open rather than sealed.
Roots like carrots sit in boxes of damp sand, packed so they never touch.
Which crop is the first to sulk if the air in there goes still?

a: One run takes four middle crates at forty centimetres, using one hundred sixty of the length.
That leaves twenty centimetres over, which no middle crate can use without an overhang.
The big crate run takes three at sixty centimetres, filling the run exactly.
Mixed runs come later, once the small crates arrive from the market stall.
Does a run of three big crates leave any usable gap at either end?
base: Carrots sulk first when the air goes still, and damp sand only slows the wilt.
The cellar tells you quickly, because still air smells of earth one day and mould the next.
Open the hatch for ten minutes on mild evenings and let the whole column turn over.
A cheap thermometer with a wire probe saves you a ladder trip every morning.
What reading range should the cellar hold through a normal winter week?

a: Print the loading day as four jobs in order, one crop at a time.
Job one is apples, job two is potatoes, job three is roots, job four is checks.
Work starts at two in the afternoon and each job takes half an hour.
The checks job needs the thermometer reading written in the notebook at the end.
Which clock time does the roots job start under that afternoon plan?
base: We can hold three to six degrees down there once the nights turn properly cold.
The notebook idea suits us, one line each morning with the reading and a word.
The first sacks go down on Saturday if the walls pass a dry hand test.
The neighbours have already asked about swapping storage space for a share of apples.
Is there any harm in letting their trays share the cellar air with ours?

a: The apples job runs from two until half past, and the potatoes follow on directly.
The potatoes finish at three, and the roots job starts at three exactly.
The roots job ends at half past three, and the checks close at four.
The last line of the day is the thermometer reading written in the notebook.
Half an hour of slack remains before the helper leaves at half past four.
The plan puts the whole loading inside two hours with no waiting between jobs.
base: Shared trays are fine if their fruit is sound, so look every tray over at the door.
One bruised apple in a dark corner can quietly spoil a whole shelf by February.
Keep their trays on a separate run so nothing of theirs touches your sand boxes.
Three to six degrees, a weekly sniff, and a full notebook will carry you to spring.
Come March, the empty crates go up the ladder and the vents stay open for the summer.

insertions.external_ungrounded: Some quiet current must carry the canal trade along, though it never once shows itself.
